Shell Asset Atlas: explainer storyboard

3:49, 10 chapters, 24 narrated lines. Every frame here is the real application, captured by film/render.py while it pressed the real controls, and the narration and timing come from film/scenes.py. Numbers come from the data built 2026-11-11.

Unofficial portfolio project. Not affiliated with, or endorsed by, Shell plc. The narration uses a synthetic voice.

0:00Public records, one globe

Shows
The app's own opening: the globe arrives from deep space over a starfield and begins to turn
Camera
No cursor. The app's fly-in runs untouched, then its idle spin. The title fades up over it.
Sound
The pad fades in under the first line.

0:00Every month, oil and gas operators tell public regulators exactly what they produced. The numbers are open to anyone. Almost no one looks.

0:10This is what happens when you put them on a globe.

0:15What the atlas is

Shows
The headline figures in the side panel: production, installations, pipelines, fuel stations
Camera
The cursor appears and passes down the figures as each is named. The globe keeps turning.
Sound
Pad only.

0:16This is the Shell Asset Atlas. It's an unofficial portfolio project, with no connection to Shell, built entirely from public data.

0:25210 installations and sites. 48 oil and gas fields. About 5,900 kilometres of pipeline. All of it drawn from regulators in the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway.

0:39Every column is a hub

Shows
Fly to the US Gulf, point at a production tower for its sparkline, click it for the full record
Camera
The cursor presses the US Gulf chip and the app flies in and tilts. It glides to the Mars tower, the hover card appears, and a click opens the details drawer.
Sound
A tick on each click.

0:39Start in the US Gulf. Each column is a production hub, and its height is what that hub produced in a month.

0:46Point at one for a quick read. Click it, and the full record opens.

0:51This is Mars: a tension-leg platform, standing in 894 metres of water since 1996.

0:59Below that, every month of production since 2015, split into liquids and gas, with a link back to the regulator's own record.

1:07A decade you can replay

Shows
The production timeline plays from the first month, the towers and the leaderboard follow, and it is paused on September 2021
Camera
The drawer is closed to reveal the leaderboard. The cursor presses play, waits on the button, and pauses on September 2021. It points at the Mars hub, then presses play again and the timeline runs to the latest month.
Sound
Ticks on play and pause.

1:09Now press play. A decade of production replays, month by month. The columns rise and fall, and the leaderboard re-ranks as it goes.

1:22Stop here: September 2021. Hurricane Ida struck at the end of August, and Shell-operated production in the Gulf fell by more than half in a single month. The Mars hub reports nothing at all.

1:35Press play again, and the recovery is there too. By December 2025, newer hubs like Vito and Whale are on the leaderboard, and the total is about a million barrels of oil equivalent a day, gross.

1:49Why it's called deepwater

Shows
The seabed basemap, colour by water depth with its legend, and search
Camera
The cursor switches the basemap to Seabed and the colours to Depth. The slash key opens search, 'Perdido' is typed and chosen, and the app flies there and begins to orbit.
Sound
Ticks on clicks and soft ticks on keys.

1:49Change the view. The seabed basemap shows why this is called deepwater: the platforms stand far beyond the continental shelf.

1:58Colour by water depth, then search for Perdido. It's moored in 2,388 metres of water.

2:05Gross is not net

Shows
The leaderboard as a way in, a partner-held field, Shell's equity in it and its net share
Camera
Escape closes the drawer. The cursor presses Troll at the top of the leaderboard and the app flies to Norway. The cursor passes over the gross and net figures, then along the chart's net line.
Sound
Ticks on clicks.

2:06The leaderboard is a way in, too. Troll, off Norway, is the biggest name on it. But Shell doesn't operate Troll. It holds about 8 percent.

2:16So the atlas marks it as a partner asset, shows Shell's net figure beside the gross one, and draws the net share as its own line. Gross is never passed off as net.

2:26Fuel stations as a skyline

Shows
The night-lights basemap, the fuel station heatmap, the 3D retail skyline and the orbit camera
Camera
Escape closes the drawer. The cursor switches to Night, presses the Europe chip, then 3D retail, and the app tilts into the skyline. Orbit starts the camera turning.
Sound
Ticks on clicks.

2:27Shell is also a name on the street. OpenStreetMap volunteers have mapped more than 28 thousand Shell-branded fuel stations.

2:36One click turns them into a skyline, where taller means more stations. Then set the camera turning.

2:44Or take the tour

Shows
The guided tour: its card, its camera moves and the record it opens at each stop
Camera
The cursor returns the map to its dark basemap, flat stations and segment colours, then presses Guided tour and steps through the first stops with Next. Escape closes the last record.
Sound
Ticks on clicks.

2:44Prefer to be shown around?

2:51The guided tour makes 12 stops, from the deepwater Gulf to a floating gas plant off Australia.

2:57Every figure in its text is computed from the data. So after each weekly refresh, the story is still true.

3:08Nothing taken on trust

Shows
Data & method: every source with its licence and fetch status, and the method notes
Camera
The cursor presses Data & method, reads down the source table, scrolls through the method notes and closes the dialog.
Sound
Ticks on clicks.

3:08And none of it has to be taken on trust. Data and method lists every source, its licence, and when it was last fetched.

3:16A pipeline rebuilds the whole atlas from those sources every week. If a regulator's site is down, it falls back to the last good copy, and says so.

3:30One globe

Shows
Back out to the whole world, then the end card with sources and the disclaimer
Camera
The cursor presses the World chip and leaves. The app flies back out to the globe and the end card fades up.
Sound
The pad fades out under the last line.

3:30The Shell Asset Atlas. Public records, one globe, and a decade you can replay.

3:36It's an unofficial project, and it isn't endorsed by Shell. The data belongs to the regulators, and to OpenStreetMap's contributors. This narration is a synthetic voice.
